prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a genuinely new idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trapping that removes the light shift on a lattice-confined ensemble, with a decade of experimental work, much of it in Ye's group, that took accuracy and stability to the 10^-18 range. The result is independently reproduced in several national laboratories and compared across institutes, so the physics is settled rather than promised. The consequences are concrete: tests of fundamental constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy, a route to redefining the second, and a many-body view of clocks. The credit is also the cleanest on the shortlist, two names with an idea-plus-realisation split that every member who ranked it accepted. Measurement capability is what limits much of experimental physics, and this is the sharpest recent advance in what we can measure and how accurately.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and appetite. The 2005 prize covered frequency combs (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize covered quantum control of single trapped ions that also underlie ion clocks, so some will see a clock prize as a third helping from the same family. Others will say a clock is a metrology instrument more than a discovery, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Credit is also not complete: Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow and Hinkley, and others made substantial contributions. On breadth, magic-angle graphene has far more first-place and top-three support than clocks, so my preferred configuration is not the one the opening ballots point to.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B038 first as a prediction matched by nature, ranks B045 fourth, and asks whether lattice clocks are an invention rather than a discovery and an extension of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
responses.response: I accept the prediction-then-observation argument for B038 and it is the strongest alternative to my own choice. But the invention-or-discovery objection does not separate the two cases: magic-wavelength trapping was a prediction that nature allowed a lattice with no differential light shift, and the experiments showed that residual systematics could be pushed below 10^-18, which is a measurement result and not just engineering. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a tool for counting optical frequency and the 2012 prize rewarded single-quantum control. Neither delivered a many-atom optical clock with this stability, which is why I treat the new prize as distinct. Where I do agree is that the priority among clock groups is genuinely unsettled, and I would not claim otherwise.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B045 first, regards the two-name credit as natural, and says the 2005 comb prize and single-ion clocks are neighbouring achievements that do not displace it.
responses.response: I agree with the core of her argument and with the two-name attribution. I would push on one point she leaves open, the overlap with ion clocks: the Al+ and Yb+ ion clocks reach similar uncertainties, and a citation should therefore stress what is specific to lattice clocks, the large atom number that gives short averaging time and access to many-body effects, so the prize does not look like a verdict between ions and lattices. We are both atomic physicists, so I would also welcome a challenge from members who do not share that vantage point about whether the clock case is as broad as we feel it is.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B016 first, judging IceCube a novel instrument that opened a new observational window, while admitting that individual credit within a collaboration is partly collective.
responses.response: The discovery is real and I take the point about an entirely new window, but the maturity and attribution arguments cut against it relative to the clocks. The diffuse flux is established, yet the sources of most of it are unresolved, and the evidence for individual sources (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still modest in significance. Naming only Halzen and Karle for a collaboration-scale result also leaves AMANDA leadership and other IceCube figures unexplained, a problem the clock configuration does not have. I would not block B016, but I do not think it should be preferred over a result that is complete, independently replicated and cleanly attributed.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B026 first, regards circuit QED as timely and mature, but notes that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits requires the committee to justify a close follow-on.
responses.response: I rank circuit QED fourth and agree that its importance is high and the architecture is now standard. My worry is the same one he names: the 2025 award is so close in subject and in the community involved that a second circuit prize within a year invites the criticism that we are recycling a field. The omission of Girvin from the credited names, whom both of us regard as a co-author of the founding proposal, adds an attribution problem that B045 does not have. If the committee decides it wants a quantum-technology prize this year, I would place trapped-ion computation (B007) ahead of B026 on timing, though I would still prefer the clock.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B038 first, calls the theory-plus-experiment split natural, and treats the unsettled superconducting pairing mechanism as something recognition need not wait for.
responses.response: I find that reasoning fair and I would not oppose B038 if the committee converges there. My reservation is the one he also records: the recognition would rest on the platform and the correlated states rather than on an understood mechanism, and the experimental side has a first-author and group-attribution question that the three-name cap cannot answer. Eight years is short for the phase diagram to settle. I am not claiming B038 is premature, only that its open questions are larger than those of clocks, and that is how I weigh the two.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a distinct achievement or as the third prize in a frequency-metrology sequence after 2005 and 2012.
Whether B038 should be preferred on breadth and opening support; the three-person cap prevents pairing it with B045 as a two-part prize without splitting a candidate's credited names.
Priority and credit among clock groups beyond Katori and Ye, which I have not verified independently.
How much weight the not-yet-completed redefinition of the second should carry.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Ye's work is closely tied to Hall's group at JILA, so a past link to the broader Boulder frequency-metrology environment may require recusal or at least disclosure on B045; the profile does not document a direct collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am also an atomic physicist in the same community as several atomic-physics candidates (B007, B028, B018), and my Lund quantum-memory and quantum-information work lies close to B007 and B028 without involving the credited names, as far as the profile shows.
